This section is meant to introduce you to some relevant vocabulary on moods so that you 
can describe your mood and that of your friends and family members. Generally, situations 
around us put us in different moods, hence knowledge of how to express these in Spanish 
will enable you to say how you feel, and how people around you feel and ask people how

Key Ideas
Dado que los estados de ánimo son situaciones temporales, se utiliza el verbo “estar” para expresar 
el estado de ánimo. ¿Cómo estás? / (¿Cómo estás?) son las formas más comunes de saber cómo

persona son ¿Qué tal te va?, ¿Qué tal estás?, ¿Cómo te sientes?, ¿Te encuentras mejor?, ¿Qué te 
pasa? y ¿Estás bien?
Las respuestas a las preguntas anteriores suelen ser: Estoy bien, Estoy triste, Estoy contento/a, 
Estoy aburrido/a, Estoy preocupado/a y Estoy nervioso/a.
Since moods are temporary situations, the verb “estar” is used in expressing one’s mood. ¿Cómo

Other expressions that can be used to find out a person’s mood are ¿Qué tal te va? (how is it going

Los Usos del Verbo “Estar”
Hay cinco usos principales del verbo “estar”. Puedes usar este acrónimo inglés “PLACE” 
para ayudarte recordarlo fácilmente.
P - Position (Posición): El verbo “estar” ayuda indicar las posiciones de objetos.
Por ejemplo, El libro está en la mesa.
L- Location (Ubicación): Usamos “estar” para indicar donde se sitúa un lugar o persona.
Por ejemplo, El supermercado está en el centro de la ciudad
Kofi está en la biblioteca
A - Action (Acción); Se usa “estar” para indicar un fenómeno que está pasando
Por ejemplo, Kabukor está comiendo.
C- Condition(Condición): Usamos “estar” para indicar el estado de una persona o un objeto.
Por ejemplo, El gato esta dormido
Apambil está cansada.
E- Estado de ánimo (Moods): Se usa “estar” para indicar como siente un individuo
Por ejemplo, Kwaku esta alegre
The Uses of the Verb “Estar”
There are five main uses of the verb, “estar”. You can use the English acronym “PLACE” 
to help you remember it easily.
P - Position (Posición): The verb “estar” helps to show the positions of objects.
For example: The book is on the table.
L- Location (Ubicación): We use “estar” to talk about where a place is situated or a person’s 
whereabouts.
For examples: The supermarket is in the centre of the city.
Kofi is in the library.
A - Action (Acción); It is used to express an ongoing event.
For example, Kabukor is eating.
C- Condition (Condición): We use “estar” to talk about the state of being of an object or a 
person.
Por ejemplo, The cat is asleep
Apambil is tired.
E- Emotions (Moods): It is used to describe the emotional state of a person

differences that exist in the Ghanaian family system and that of the Hispanic world.

Key Ideas 
Palabras como «una familia nuclear/una familia extendida» describen los sistemas familiares 
generales que existen en Ghana y en el mundo hispano. El tamaño de la familia puede ser grande 
o pequeño (una familia grande o pequeña). También hay familias monoparentales y familias 
biparentales. Un valor familiar importante tanto en el sistema familiar ghanés como en el del 
mundo hispano es el respeto de los mayores. Esto es evidente incluso en el uso de «usted» en la 
lengua española. Las religiones principales en Ghana son la tradicional, el cristianismo a y el islam. 
En el mundo hispano, la religión dominante es el cristianismo, principalmente el catolicismo. En

Words like “una familiar nuclear/ una familiar extendida” (nuclear and extended family) 
describe the general family systems that exist in Ghana and the Hispanic world. The family size 
can be big or small (una familiar grande o pequena). There are also families comprising single 
parents(monoparentales) and families with both parents(biparental). One major family value in 
both the Ghanaian family system and that of the Hispanic world is respect for the elderly (respecto 
de los mayores). This is evident in the use of the “usted” in the Spanish language. The main 
religions in Ghana are the traditional, Christianity and Islam. In the Hispanic world, the dominant 
religion is Christianity, mainlyCatholicism. In terms of marriage, polygamous marriage can be 
found in Ghana but it is almost non-existent in the Hispanic world.

Family Structure in Ghana and the Spanish-Speaking World
In Ghana, the family structure has traditionally been very broad and centred around 
the extended family. In many Ghanaian communities, it is common for multiple family 
members, including grandparents, uncles, aunts, and cousins, to live together or close 
to each other. This system fosters a support network where children are cared for not 
only by their parents but also by other relatives. The extended family plays a crucial 
role in raising children and passing down cultural values and traditions.
In rural areas of Ghana, families tend to be large, with many children, as children are 
considered a blessing and a source of support for parents in their old age. However, 
in urban areas, families are beginning to adopt smaller structures due to factors 
such as urbanization, education, and the cost of living. Despite these changes, family 
values and traditions remain fundamental in Ghanaian society.
On the other hand, in the Spanish-speaking world, the family structure has undergone 
significant transformations in recent decades. Traditionally, families in Spanish-
speaking countries were also extended, with multiple generations living together or 
in close proximity. However, nowadays, the nuclear family, consisting of parents and 
their children, has become more common, especially in urban areas.
In many Spanish-speaking countries, family size has decreased, with fewer children 
compared to previous generations. This is partly due to the influence of modernization, 
education, and the increasing participation of women in the workforce. Although the 
nuclear family is now more common, connections with the extended family remain 
strong, with frequent family gatherings and celebrations that reinforce family bonds.
A notable difference between the two family systems is the role of religion in family 
life. In Ghana, religious traditions, both Christian and Muslim, are fundamental 
and often dictate family practices, including marriage and child-rearing. In many 
Spanish-speaking countries, Catholicism has historically been a unifying force in the 
family, although in recent years there has been an increase in religious diversity and 
greater secularisation.
In summary, although both in Ghana and in the Spanish-speaking world the family 
remains a central institution, family dynamics have changed over time. In Ghana, the 
extended family remains predominant, especially in rural areas, while in the Spanish-
speaking world, the nuclear family has gained importance. However, in both contexts, 
family values and traditions continue to play a vital role in society.

Introduction(Introducción)
Esta sección te permitirá saber cómo saludar, cómo responder a los saludos y cómo despedirse 
de los demás. Dado que el saludo es parte integrante de la cultura ghanesa, es necesario 
que conozcas y comprendas cómo se realiza en la lengua que estás aprendiendo. También 
es esencial saber que en el mundo hispano se distingue entre saludar a los compañeros 
(informal) y a los adultos o extraños (formal).
This section is to enable you to know how to greet, how to respond to greetings and how 
to take leave of others. Since greeting is an integral part of the Ghanaian culture, it is 
necessary for you to know and understand how it is done in the language that you are 
learning. It is also essential to know that in the Hispanic world, a distinction is made 
between greeting peers (informal) and adults or strangers(formal).
At the end of this section, you should be able to (Al final de esta sección, 
deberías ser capaz de):
1.  Escuchar y observar amigos que se saludan
2.  Saludar y despedirte de los amigos/las amigas/los compañeros/las compañeras. (Expresión 
oral -informal/tú)
3.  Saludar y despedirte de la gente mayor/ extranjeros/extranjeras. (Expresión oral-formal/
usted)
Key Ideas 
 There are two ways of greeting people in Spanish namely the formal and informal. Hola and 
¿cómo estás? are used when you are greeting your peers (informal) while ¿cómo está usted? 
is used for adults and strangers (formal). Buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches are used 
depending on the time of day. Adiós and Hasta Luego are the most common ways of saying 
goodbye.

Key Ideas
En español, “time” es «la hora», por eso se utilice el artículo definido femenino para decir la hora. 
Para decir la hora se utiliza el verbo «ser». Sólo se utiliza «es» cuando la hora es la una, a partir 
de las dos se utiliza «son». Además, cuando la hora es la una, el artículo definido utilizado es «la», 
mientras que «las» se utiliza a partir de las dos. Al preguntar por la hora, decimos «¿qué hora es?» 
o «¿a qué estamos?». La respuesta suele ser «es la... o son las...». Si es por la mañana, se añade «de 
la mañana», por la tarde, «de la tarde» y por la noche, «de la noche».
In Spanish, time is “la hora” hence the feminine definite article is used in saying time. The verb 
“ser” is used in saying time. “es” is used only when the time is one o’clock, from two o’clock 
onwards, “son” is used. In addition, when the time is one o’clock, the definite article used is “la” 
whereas “las” is used when the time is two o’clock onwards. In asking for the time, we say “qué  
hora es?” or “a qué  estamos?”. The response is usually, “es la… or son las…” If it is in the 
morning, add “de la manana”, in the afternoon, “de la tarde” and in the evening, “de la noche”.
• La hora (the time) is feminine so the feminine definite articles (la/las) are used to say the 
time.
• Es la una = It’s one o’clock
• Son las dos/tres/cuatro etc. = It’s two/three/four o’clock
• Key question: ¿qué hora es?
• Use“de la mañana” if it’s in the morning, “de la tarde” if it’s in the afternoon/evening and 
“de la noche” if it’s at night.

LA HORA
En español, decimos la hora con los artículos definidos femeninos y los números. Usamos 
la y las con el número. Es importante saber que usamos “la” solo para el número uno en 
la forma femenina. 
In Spanish, we say the time with the feminine definite articles and numbers. We use la and 
las with the number. It’s important to know that we only use la with number 1 in it’s femine 
form (when it’s 1 o’clock)
Por ejemplo, La una - 1 o’clock
 Las tres - 3 o’clock
 Las cinco – 5 o’clock

same time. The subject is the same as the object. It is usually accompanied by a reflexive 
pronoun. These are the types of verbs that are used to write and talk about daily routines

LOS APELLIDOS EN EL MUNDO HISPÁNICO
Generally, in Ghana, we take our surnames from our father. So, your father’s surname 
automatically becomes your surname. If Mr. Kafui Letsa has a son called Mawuli, 
automatically his surname will be Letsa hence Mawuli Letsa.
In the Hispanic world, however, people use two family names (apellidos): their father’s 
family name and their mother’s maiden name. For instance, if Francisco Marzón and 
Gema Galván give birth to a son called Juan, the son’s surname will be Marzon Galvan 
hence Juan Marzón Galván. In future, should Juan Marzón Galván get married to Dora 
Rodríguez Rivera and have a daughter by the name of María, their daughter’s surname will 
be Galván Rodríguez, hence María Galván Rodríguez.

This section focuses on how to describe the people around us. After being introduced to 
vocabulary on family members, you are going to use that knowledge to now describe their 
physical appearance and character. This can be achieved by knowing the vocabulary 
associated with people’s physique and character, the use of “ser”, adjectives and articles. 
At the end of this section, you will be able to:

Key Ideas
Para describir a una persona se utiliza el verbo “ser”. “Ser” se utiliza con adjetivos como “alto/a”, 
“delgado/a”, “bajo/a” y “gordo/a” para describir el físico de una persona. Para decir el carácter 
de una persona, utilice el verbo “ser” y adjetivos que describan el carácter de las personas como 
“simpático/a”, “majo/a”, “amistoso/a”, etc. También es importante señalar que “un/una/unos” 
y “unas” (a or an) son los artículos indefinidos en español. Los artículos definidos en español son 
“el/la/los/las”. 
When describing people, the verb “ser” (to be) is used. “Ser” is used with adjectives such as 
“alto/a” (tall), “delgado/a” (slim), “bajo/a” (short), and “gordo/a” (big) to describe someone’s 
physique. To tell a person’s character, use the verb “ser” and adjectives describing people’s 
character such as “simpático/a” (kind), “majo/a” (nice), “amistoso/a” (friendly), etc. It is also 
worth noting that “un/una/unos” and “unas” (a or an) are the Spanish indefinite articles. The 
definite articles in Spanish are “el/la/los/las” (the).

LOS ADJETIVOS 
En español, como en inglés, para hacer una descripción de una persona o miembro de la 
familia, usamos adjetivos. Estos adjetivos se usan según el género y número del sustantivo 
a que se refiere. 
To describe a person or a family member, adjectives are used. These adjectives are used in 
accordance with the number and gender of the noun they describe.
Ahora, vamos a ver algunas reglas
Now, we are going to see some rules.
1. La mayoría de los adjetivos españoles siguen al sustantivo que califican. 
Most Spanish adjectives come after the noun they qualify. 
Ejemplos; 
A red backpack = Una mochila roja. (in actual sense it means a backpack red)
A blue pencil = Un lápiz azul
A white house= Una casa blanca 
A green shirt = Una camisa verde
2.  El adjetivo debe concordar en número y género con el sustantivo al que califica. The 
adjective must agree in gender and number with the noun it qualifies. 
Ejemplos; 
The beautiful girl= La chica bonita 
The beautiful girls= Las chicas bonitas 
A Ghanaian boy = Un chico ghanés
The rich women = Las mujeres ricas
3. Los adjetivos que describen cantidad siempre van delante del sustantivo.   Adjectives 
of quantity always come before the noun. 
Ejemplos; 
Three books = Tres libros 
Four cars = Cuatro coches
Some few things = Unas pocas cosas
So much light = Tanta luz
A lot of money = Mucho dinero
We have enough food to eat = Tenemos bastante comida para comer
